title: "Inside Out" and the Neuroscience of Emotion (my conflicted thoughts)

commenti.body:
I don't agree that the original movie was inspired by that psychological theory. I think it was inspired by popular American models of mind, and I saw it be incredibly valuable for my own child in developing a theory of mind - an idea of how her mind worked.

Was that model especially accurate? I don't believe so, but I don't think that matters.

I am an existentialist, and so I believe these theories are constructs to enable us to survive the fundamental challenges of life, not searches for objective truths. And so in an individual's life, these models are iterated upon, become more nuanced, hopefully avoid essentialist and simplistic explanations, and help our lives - because the process of developing one's theory of mind and philosophy is valuable, as well as the results.

Essentially, philosophical and psychological insights into humanity can be a way to improve our lives, not only an arrow aimed at Truth. Because, as Camus said, “There is only one really serious philosophical problem, and that is suicide,”

Neurologists seeking material explanations for all psychological phenomena is, well, tautologous. If they valued non-material explanations based on theories of mind, they wouldn't be neurologists. But I do value non-material explorations of the human psyche, and believe the process that all humans - non-neurologists - undertake is tremendously valuable. And I think these movies are, as lightly philosophical art rather than neurological research papers, tremendously valuable.

Words are not simply metaphors. The neurological facts of the brain are physics and biology, voltages and biochemistry. In science, the words we use (such as the names of emotions) are imperfect things used to flail at empirical facts of a different class. However, in general life, words are part of how we conceive and construct our selves, and how we survive the terrifying chasm that is life without an authority that tells us how to be human.

I take umbrage with you dismissing the film by saying “it’s for kids”. Clearly the audience for both films was stacked high with adults of all ages, ethnicities, and countries of origin, most going without kids. And as far as the medium goes, I would hope you don’t think animated films are automatically for children.

I also don’t think it’s fair to ask a film like this to be an educational film that’s illustrating the currently vogue neuroscience theories. It is, as you said, a fantasy film that’s got to construct its own rules and logic. Theories of mind no doubt inspired the initial concept, but of course it wasn’t going to stick to that. 

Still, I’d like to read more reviews of the film from a neuroscience perspective.

I agree with you, but mostly because there was a lot of hoopla about how it was based on science when it came out.

I thought I was going crazy when people were lauding it for this, because to me it seemed so oversimplified that it may as well have just been a creative idea rather than being based on science.

Whether it’s helpful for kids or not depends on the kid I would say. I think there’s a lot of psuedoscientific commentary available on this. At the end of the day it’s a simple kids movie with a premise that is neither original not groundbreaking (previous iterations of this same idea have appeared in British comics since the 50s).

It's very dishonest to respond with "animated film aren't necessarily for children" when that's not what he said. This particular film is for children, which is just inarguable.

It's true where we live in a culture where adults regularly watch children's films on their own, but that doesn't change what the film is.
Wasn't that just marketing? Marketing is lies, it's not worth engaging with.

"neuroscientists have also been moving away from viewing the adolescent brain as a sharply distinct phase in brain development, and instead as part of a long process of brain development that begins at birth and passes through gradual phases until death"

Source for this statement?

Physiology or neurology aside, the adolescent brain is self-evidently going through a major shift in emotional development. Pretty much anybody who remembers their teenage years, or has parented or experienced a teenager between the years of 11-14 knows that the emotional development during that time period is like a thunderstorm of change.

It's definitely a personal pet peeve, but I can't stand stories that mechanize the human body to personify the processes within it. Especially the human brain, because I (too) like to study psychology and biological psychological science. To me, it feels like it flattens the real wonder and science behind the very cool things happening in our bodies that fuel us and puts it in a pointlessly suburban and unnatural context. It doesn't feel creative to me, it just feels lazy, because the science is never really accurate or good. You can't say you're enticing your children to learn more when they get inspired by something that is factually incorrect. I get that films aren't trying to be textbooks or primarily educational, or whatever, it's a taste thing, but it's just foundationally against my own tastes and weirdly has been since I was a child.

I don't mind humans shrunk down to explore the human body stories though. Cells at Work : NO. Innerspace : YES.

>I just wish it portrayed emotions with the same complexity and depth. Instead, **we are left with the idea of emotions as fixed and unchanging.**

I don't think we are. >!Joy and Anxiety both learned that you can't control everything. Joy had to stop trying to block the bad stuff (which was kinda what she did in the first movie) and Anxiety learned you can't control everything. Joy cries at one point. Even Embarrassment kind of stepped out and tried taking control at a couple times rather than staying scared in the background.!< There might be more beyond that, but those are the ones I recall off-hand.

This was an interesting read, thanks. Although I found the original Inside Out flawed in its structure, I was ultimately strongly moved by the film. Obviously it wanted the model of human emotional development it was constructing to be informative or useful in some way, but I don't think its goal was to provide an accurate depiction of the workings of the human mind. I think it was aiming to teach a lesson on the value of sadness. Sadness is uncomfortable for parents. They may find their child's sadness intolerable and seek ways to eliminate it from his or her experience. This is especially true in the modern age when many parents have limited time to spend with their children. They want the time they do have to be happy - understandable. The film warns of the dangers of sadness going unrecognised and suggests an important, constructive role sadness can play in development. The lesson is for children too - it's OK to be sad sometimes. It's a simple message, but a very important one. I found the theme of honouring our sadness very moving.

>Was that model especially accurate? I don't believe so, but I don't think that matters.

"All models are wrong, but some are useful."

> And I think these movies are, as lightly philosophical art rather than neurological research papers, tremendously valuable.

This is an interesting idea. There is a natural expectation that art will not be constrained by scientific rigor or accuracy. A parallel phenomenon exists with historicity. People differ with respect to how much this matters. Does it matter if a story about the life of Abe Lincoln takes artistic license if the goal is to tell an important story with important themes, even if they don't reflect the actual dialogue/events of the historical person Abe Lincoln? I think reasonable viewers can and do disagree on this point. 

I like the OP's exploration of the accuracy of the cognitive model presented. Your child's development being enhanced by the film isn't really in conflict with OP's point that the film can have positive benefits for children given it will enhance their ability to conceptually engage with their emotions and the concept of a self. 

I do think it's common to take complex ideas and simplify them down to tell a story. I think while this is expedient and makes for clean storytelling, I personally think we should also aspire for as much nuance and accuracy and even rigor to be preserved as possible. By way of analogy, the best war stories to me are those that grapple with war as it is (a hard challenge) and not as it is romanticized (far easier and lends itself to sweeping, epic, and even moving storytelling). I admire the spirit of a critique that our depiction of our internal cognitive state should similarly be closer the best of our scientific knowledge at this time. It challenges those who create art, it challenges our audience, and it provides us a constant source of growth as our creations must change and adapt just as our understanding of the world is constantly doing the same.

I appreciate you adding your existentialist philosophical perspective. I agree that the film can probably be a useful construct, even though I'd argue it is overly essentialist. 

Just one thing I wanted to point out: I searched this topic after posting the review, and I see that Inside Out was actually created directly under the guidance of the Paul Eckman who popularized the six basic emotions [https://time.com/6987825/inside-out-2-neuroscience/](https://time.com/6987825/inside-out-2-neuroscience/) I know you said you're not as interested in the science, but for anyone else reading this - the article claims that the film does reflect real neuroscience, but a lot of Eckman's research has actually been undermined by later findings. He is most famous for visiting people from many cultures, showing them images of stereotypical facial expressions, and documenting that they were able to match them to the basic emotions. However, later studies found that this only works when subjects were provided multiple choices. As mentioned in my post, it is also now clear that there aren't any specific areas of the brain that are dedicated to processing specific emotions. I wouldn't say discrete emotion theory has been debunked, but a lot of its tenets face are strongly challenged by the evidence.

It really isn’t. I’m sick of this sub dismissing animation with children in it as primarily or even only for kids. My theatre was 90% adults when I went, and it was sold out. Walt Disney himself said they didn’t make films for children, only films children could enjoy, too. 

The pretension and dismissal of the medium and art of animation is ridiculous.

I’m too sleepy to give a substantial answer, but I’m curious as to why you exclusively use ‘neuroscience’ rather than ‘psychology’ in your discourse. To me neuroscience is one part of psychology, but I wonder if our perspective is the same?

I’d also add that, to me, Time magazine isn’t a source of real information. I don’t mind you summarising things you know because you’re a practicing neurologist or just a lay person who’s interested, because you seem honest, but to me Time is a negative source - less authoritative than just hearsay - because it’s part of the marketing machine, and just not honest at all.

I’m not uninterested in science - my work is partly social science - I just think that the narrative that Inside Out is based on science is questionable.

There’s a lot to unpack there. You seem to be saying that science is the sole source of truth. I’ve worked in linguistics and social science most of my adult life, and grown up around it. I’m not anti-science in the slightest.

I don’t think ‘there’s an expectation that art will not be constrained by scientific rigor or accuracy’ is a very coherent idea.

Firstly artistic texts are not scientific texts. They are not constrained by scientific rigor any more than any non-scientific text. They may have rigor or not, they may challenge or not, but they aren’t trying to be science so they don’t fail its requirements.

Accuracy is complex. Good texts are trying to be accurate - to conform to reality - but which aspects of reality is much more complex. For example, fantasy fiction often requires a realistic approach to relationships and human challenges, otherwise it’s entirely fictional and uninteresting. Similarly, popular historical narratives are not facts. They are merely what we think happened, and part of a narrative on the past. This is why real historians *continually* engage in historical revisionism, to the chagrin of a lay public that believes the are magically changing the facts of the past - which of course we have little empirical access to.

Basically, I feel as if you are saying this work (as light and slight as it is) is not trying to be truthful at all, when I believe it is, but that truthfulness is more complex and has many more aspects than those you mention.

But I’m sorry if I am misreading you. It’s early and I haven’t had any coffee.

> Firstly artistic texts are not scientific texts. They are not constrained by scientific rigor any more than any non-scientific text. They may have rigor or not, they may challenge or not, but they aren’t trying to be science so they don’t fail its requirements.

While that's true, and while I also think science does not have a monopoly on truth, it does present a lens through which we can access and evaluate purported knowledge. In this way, artistic texts can be in conversation with scientific texts, or at the very least juxtaposed to them. Whether we use the word "constraint" or something else, I think what matters is the extent to which one could apply a "scientific lens" to the artistic text and find coherence there. 

Put another way, religious texts are not constrained by science per se, but one can say that splitting a single loaf of bread into a hundred is not coherent with our understand of mass conservation. Whether it says something about the Truth or historicity of that episode is up for debate. 

I find that some art wants to have their cake and eat it too--to be scientifically revealing (or to carry a pastiche of "scienciness") but at the same time to be sufficiently elevated in the realm of art as to be above critique on mere scientific grounds. I'm not opposed to it per se, mostly because, as you say, artistic texts are not scientific texts, but I think it is nevertheless worth addressing any supposed or perceived scientific underpinnings which may reasonably influence one's appraisal of the art with all its parts taken together. 

> Basically, I feel as if you are saying this work (as light and slight as it is) is not trying to be truthful at all, when I believe it is, but that truthfulness is more complex and has many more aspects than those you mention.
> 
> But I’m sorry if I am misreading you. It’s early and I haven’t had any coffee.

I hope the above reveals that I'm not saying this. If that was not clear, your lack of coffee is met with my long surpassed bedtime. I think truthfulness is indeed complex, and I also don't think truthfulness is necessarily a standard by which this work (or many works) need to be appraised for the work to be excellent (and effective and moving and instructive). But I do think that scientific truth is an element worth interrogating, and that this is not terribly hard to do (any more so than establishing historical accuracy or internal logical consistency, etc).

I only cited Time because they mention that Paul Ekman advised on the film. 

I think I've been using the word neuroscience too loosely. There is a lot of overlap between neuroscience and psychology, but Ekman's cultural studies fall much more closely into psychology. Neuroscience is the study of the nervous system and the brain. The brain is involved in almost every aspect of bodily function - thoughts and emotions are just one small part of what the brain does. In contrast, psychology specifically studies the mind and behavior. They usually are not studying the brain directly, but are instead inferring what is happening in the mind based on behaviors and expressed attitudes. 

There has been a big leap in neuroscience associated with the use of fMRI, a tool which allows researchers to assign subjects a task and then study which areas of the brain were disproportionately activated and excited while they performed that task. This is how they can see how emotions manifest in the actual wiring of the brain, and findings like this are likely to be published in a neuroscience journal. This is just one tool neuroscientists use to study the brain. On the other hand, the cross-cultural studies I mentioned where people are asked about emotion in facial expressions are likely to be published in a psychology journal.

I am interested in both neuroscience and psychology, but I have been particularly interested recently in what we know and don't know about how the brain works, whether that's in relation to emotion, predictive processing, animal brains, placebo effects, optical illusions, brain development, etc. I did not study this in school and I am not an expert. I actually went to school for a social science myself. I just read about this topic because I find it fascinating.

I don't want to overstate the case, since neuroscientists would still generally characterize adolescence as a phase in brain development. But the changes that are observed in the brain at the onset of adolescence are as gradual as at any other point in a person's life (you can read the charts) [https://web.archive.org/web/20230506212051/https://www.washingtonpost.com/wellness/2023/02/28/brain-aging-childhood-teens-adults/](https://web.archive.org/web/20230506212051/https://www.washingtonpost.com/wellness/2023/02/28/brain-aging-childhood-teens-adults/) Original source here [https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-022-04554-y](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-022-04554-y) There is a period of extremely rapid change and growth in the brain, but that is during infancy, not puberty.

Thanks for the nice post.

Don't worry, I know MRIs, I've translated MRI tech manuals, and had a gazillion myself, though not fMRIs.

I'm interested too, but like you, not a pro. I'm old, so I've picked up a lot of info over the years, separately from what I studied in The Before Times. I don't have journal access currently, but I used to have paid access to lots of academic journals, and that's a way I like to learn - from reading papers, not books - or videos.

Yeah, that's all very sensible and smart. Thank you.

I agree that some art wants to use science in that way, but I tend to separate what the marketing does from what the text does. So if Riley was having fMRIs and it was making the emotion characters vibrate or run from the waves, I'd start noticing that dissonance. Marketing claims made by the creators - or more specifically by the marketing team employed by the same corporation as the creators - are just background noise to me. Or at least I try to make them become background noise.

So I don't really see that as the art writing scientific checks it can't cash.

The movie clearly simplifies the workings of human emotion, so children *specifically* can understand, as a story about the emotions of a *child*. If you have something like Grave of the Fireflies, then it's a different story, but Inside Out is just clearly a children's movie, like plenty of live-action movies also are.
Child-friendly isn’t the same thing as for children primarily. Or are you calling Pete Doctor a liar when he repeated Walt’s words about making films kids can watch, but not kid’s films?

A "Children's Movie" isn't the necessarily the same as or "For Children Primarily", and many movies that are "Child-Friendly" aren't "Children's Movies". Plenty can be enjoyed by adults. Ultimately, most labeling for genre and such things are just that, constructs. But in this case, Inside Out fits the general definition of a children's movie. It focuses on the experiences of a child, and it is partly intended to teach children about these complex subjects that most adults understand. I don't see how acknowledging the fact is *dismissive* towards animation. If anything, you're being dismissive towards children's movies. 

It is unfortunate that people dismiss animation, it is partly because of the industry using the medium a lot of the time as an excuse to pump out formulaic and mediocre pictures, which are "children's films" primarily because the "child" audience doesn't question the quality. But that doesn't mean the "Children's Film" is a mediocre genre. So isn't pushing back against the animation stigma in this way just going to create a separate stigma about "Children's Films", that animation is so much "above" them?

I’m not sure I understand your point about the Time article? You say that the film wasn’t based off of Ekman’s emotions theory. But the article is an interview with a scientist who consulted on the film (as did Ekman) who says that the emotions were chosen based on Ekman’s theory. So it seems to me like the scientific consultants had a measurable impact on the film.

I thought it was clear - I'm saying that this is part of the marketing machine, just like Youtube interviews where they talk about what a fun time they had on set. I have no idea what the truth is, because marketing people lie, magazines lie, media lies, advertising lies. I work with marketing people every day. Dishonesty is such a huge part of that industry that most participants don't even see it as dishonesty. It's just work making words.

That is a scientist purported to have said those words, but this isn't a scientific paper, focusing on replicability and downplaying the authority of the author. Just the marketing machine trying to get butts into the theater/bums on seats.

This is one aspect of Barthes' tremendous insights in Death of the Author. We don't have access to the mind of the artist. Given the existence of the subconscious, even *the artist* doesn't have full access. 

Add Hollywood and capitalism to that mix, and we find that we are in a state of ignorance about art creation so terrifying to art-lovers (of any medium) that many refuse to accept how little they truly know.
